title: Adaptive plans add 0.0625 expected constraints at 16 attempts in an independent Allen mouse delay-recovery model
abstract: We tested whether outcomes from early delay-recovery attempts can improve later measurement choices. We repeated the graph extraction for Allen Synaptic Physiology r2.1. The primary mouse design has twelve single requirements and four disjoint two-delay requirements for new tests of an additive cell-delay model. This structure repeats a prior campaign result. Under independent equal recovery chance 0.5, exact dynamic programming gives 6.5625 expected added constraints with at most sixteen adaptive attempts. The best fixed plan gives 6.5. The gain is 0.0625 constraints, or 0.96 percent. At this chance, the largest gain across all tested budgets is 0.21875 at seventeen attempts. Strict labels give the same gain curve shifted by five attempts. Human recovery adds no constraint. An independent labeled-edge recursion and exhaustive fixed-plan checks pass 180 small-instance comparisons with exact fractions. This is a small conditional design benefit, not new evidence about neuronal timing. Recovery chances, outcome independence and equal costs are assumptions. No missing delays were recovered. Code, aggregate counts, source provenance and external regeneration steps support reproduction; external records are excluded.

display.caption: Exact expected added constraints at recovery chance 0.5. Adaptive choices use earlier success or failure outcomes. Fixed choices are set before attempts. Both have the same maximum attempt budget.

citations.reason: Prior fixed-plan recovery benchmark and requirement decomposition. We repeat source extraction and add adaptive outcome-based planning.
Shows why failure dependence matters in the same model setting.
